# Draft:Edward(Ed) Higgens (Artist)

Edward Higgins was a surrealist and abstract artist operating in the Bay Area and the Sacramento Valley. He was Born in San Bernadino California. After high school he attended Santa Rosa's Junior college, graduating with an Associates degree in the arts in 1959. He later transferred into Chico State with a Bachelor's degree in the arts in 1960. Finally finding his way to UC Davis's masters of fine arts program, graduating in 1969. Ed Higgins' art career started with a focus on surrealism. His subjects throughout 1969 to 1980's were surreal and fantastical interpretations of the countryside around the Carquinez Strait. Later on he gained a new interest and fascination of a range of simplistic to intricate, abstract patterns.
Higgins notably worked closely and was friends with some of UC Davis' original arts department founders, like Robert Arneson, William T. Wiley and Roy De Forest.
Diablo Valley College
In 1970 Ed Higgins was working as one of three painting instructors at Diablo Valley College. The art department were operating out of transformed, retired army barracks. Higgins had a reputation of being a committed and dedicated teacher, giving his students ample time to do their work. Also working with smaller classes of 15 - 20 students who each were set up with their own easel. He had an understanding and agreeable teaching style as described by some of his students. He was very popular for the freedom he gave his students in the classroom. He also brought in live models working with the San Francisco and Oakland Modeling Guild.
Higgins utilized an interesting method to his lectures in the classroom, in class he would have his students view and discuss reference paintings to help them contextualize assignments. Higgins also made an effort to expose his students to modern art early on in their careers. Instead of just looking to the past, only having the paintings of Da Vinci, Picasso, Van Gogh, Rockwell and Calder to look to, and be the extent of their knowledge and inspiration. Instead he gave his students opportunities and examples of other sources of inspiration that were more relevant during the time.
Higgins made an effort in the classroom to foster collaboration and learning among peers. He would ask his students what they learned from the assignment, but also asked them how can they improve or what else they could've learned if they were focused on something.
